first.rationale: Two of the three current problems are internal funnel decay (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%), and the inherited record has two independent, mutually reinforcing entries pointing at the onboarding funnel (memory_86 on shortened onboarding, memory_31 on signup field reduction), plus memory_91 on in-product activation messaging as an adjacent lever. Fixing the funnel compounds across every acquisition channel and is the most consistent with 'sustainable long-term qualified revenue,' whereas promotional_pricing (memory_73) is the reflexive answer to the competitor's entry pricing but buys acquisition with margin and anchors a price-sensitive cohort at a discounted rate — the memory reports acquisition and revenue lift but says nothing about retention, renewal price realization, or lifetime value, so it is the highest downstream-value risk of the five. I am spending verification on memory_86 because it is the memory my intended action rests on most directly (I need the original record to know whether the lift was measured on completion rate alone or on downstream qualified revenue, and how old and how large the sample was), and on memory_73 because it is the strongest competing pull this week and I want the original record to show whether the revenue lift was gross or net of discount and whether retention was actually measured rather than merely 'not measurably harmed.' I am not verifying memory_31, which overlaps memory_86 and would waste the budget on redundant confirmation. Two caveats I am carrying forward rather than resolving: these are consolidated summaries from days 12-61, and conditions have changed materially by day 76 — a competitor entrant alters the counterfactual, so prior effect sizes should be treated as upper bounds, not forecasts. Also, memory_44 says enterprise converts through sales-assisted, demo-request flows; cutting required signup fields is exactly the change that can degrade lead qualification and routing, so the experiment must preserve the enterprise demo path and instrument pipeline quality, not just activation counts. If memory_86 turns out to have measured only completion rate with no revenue linkage, or if memory_73's record shows genuine net-of-discount retention data, I will downgrade to a small guarded test or reconsider the pricing response.

final.rationale:
Verification resolved both questions decisively and in opposite directions. exp_86 came back stronger than the consolidated summary implied: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and crucially 30-day retention +3% — so the onboarding lift is not a vanity funnel metric, it survives into retained accounts, which is exactly the linkage to sustainable qualified revenue I needed. exp_73 came back materially worse than its summary: the consolidated memory_73 said 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' and omitted 30-day retention -12% and an explicit source-record warning not to generalize targeted discounting. The acquired cohort does not survive first renewal, so the +18% qualified revenue is largely borrowed against churn. That is a consolidation distortion, and I am flagging it: memory_73 as written would have led a future session straight into the competitor-response trap. It should be corrected in durable memory, and its sibling summaries (memory_57's 'no measurable harm to retention', which is the same soft phrasing pattern) should be treated as unverified until someone pulls exp_57.

Decision: simplify_onboarding, standard experiment. It directly addresses two of the three live problems (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%), it is the only candidate with a verified retention-positive record, and funnel improvements compound across all acquisition channels rather than buying one discounted cohort. I am deliberately not answering the competitor's entry pricing with price. Losing some price-sensitive SMB accounts to a discounter is cheaper than acquiring a cohort that churns at renewal; the verified evidence says matching on price destroys value.

Uncertainty I am carrying rather than resolving: exp_86 ran under pre-competitor conditions, so I treat +13%/+3% as an upper bound, not a forecast. Its retention readout is 30-day, which does not reach a renewal cycle — exactly the horizon where exp_73 fell apart — so I will instrument this experiment through at least one renewal window before anyone calls it confirmed or scales it. Guardrails: preserve the enterprise demo-request path intact when cutting signup fields (memory_44 says sales-assisted flows carry pipeline quality, and field reduction is the classic way to degrade lead routing and qualification), and measure qualified pipeline and renewal-cycle retention as primary outcomes, not activation counts alone. memory_91's activation messaging is the natural follow-on next slot; I am not bundling it, so the onboarding effect stays attributable.
